author: Montesquieu
excerpt: Nor is there liberty if the power of judging is not separate from legislative power and from executive power. If it were joined to legislative power, the power over the life and liberty of the citizens would be arbitrary, for the judge would be the legislator. If it were joined to executive power, the judge could have the force of an oppressor.  All would be lost if the same man or the same body of principal men — either of nobles or of the people — exercised these three powers: that of making the laws, that of executing public resolutions, and that of judging the crimes or disputes of individuals.  In the governments of Europe, there are three powers: legislative, executive, and judicial. The liberty of the citizen depends upon their separation. When combined in one hand — or in one body — tyranny results.

The land question is perhaps the most important and the most contentious of all our social problems. Land is the material basis of economic life. By depriving Africans of the free enjoyment and use of their land, the colonial system strikes at the economic independence of the African and makes him a serf or a vassal

title: Giuseppe Mazzini — On the Duties of Man, Essay on Nationalism

Evil governments have disfigured the Divine design by their conquests, their greed, and their jealousy.  May each one of you, fortified by the power and affection of many millions, all speaking the same language, gifted with the same tendencies, and educated by the same historical tradition, hope even by your own single efforts to be able to benefit all Humanity.  O, my brothers, love your Country! Our country is our Home, a house God has given us, placing therein a numerous family that loves us, and whom we love; a family with whom we sympathize more readily and whom we understand more quickly than we do others. title: Japanese Colonization of Korea — Cultural Erasure Policy
author: Radio Korea International (secondary account)
excerpt: In order to make Koreans just like the Japanese, the Korean people were forced to change their family names into Japanese names. In religious life, Japan forced the Korean people to worship the Japanese gods as a part of their duty.  This policy was aimed at erasing the Korean nation — the cultural identity — from the earth forever and to nurture them as colonial subjects and slaves obedient only to the Japanese.  Ultimately, the Japanese drew countless Korean youths and women to the battle fields, factories, and mines to aid in their conquests and wars.  This forced cultural assimilation — the destruction of language, names, religion, and national identity — is what Kim Il-sung's Juche ideology was explicitly built to resist and prevent from ever happening again.

equity_note: This document directly explains the origin of North Korea's isolationist Juche ideology — it was a response to having every marker of Korean identity systematically destroyed. Reading it alongside Kim Il-sung's speech (document 3b in your G2.01 Enduring Issues set) creates powerful cause-and-effect analysis. The cultural erasure policy (renaming, forced religious practice, conscript labor) is a textbook case of colonial identity destruction. In countries where these associations do not exist, if private individuals are unable to create some kind of permanent tie between themselves, tyranny will increase and the rest will remain powerless in front of it.  American freedom of association is one of the most efficacious weapons they possess. The first time I heard in the United States that a hundred thousand men had bound themselves publicly to abstain from spirituous liquors, it appeared to me more like a joke than a serious engagement, and I did not at once perceive why these temperate citizens could not content themselves with dri

His observation that political freedom depends on the right to associate freely is prescient — the destruction of this right is what made Jim Crow possible after Reconstruction. title: Al-Muqaddimah — On Group Solidarity and the Rise of Dynasties
author: Ibn Khaldun

When a dynasty arises, it progresses through stages. At first, it is based on strength and solidarity. Later, it becomes accustomed to luxury and ease. Then, as time passes, the members of the dynasty lose their toughness and become dependent on others for protection.  The desert people are closer to goodness than sedentary people, because they are further removed from luxury and corruption. Civilization ('umran) grows, but with it comes moral decay. title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman — On Education and Equality
author: Mary Wollstonecraft
excerpt: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves. The mind will ever be unstable that has only prejudices to rest on. Women are told from their infancy that beauty is woman's sceptre, and the mind shapes itself to the body. Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience.  They who are to be the educators of children ought to be themselves educated. If women are not prepared by education to become the companions of men, they will stop the progress of knowledge and virtue. Society must change its view of women. They are not naturally inferior, but appear so because they lack education.  Let women share the advantages of education and rational instruction, and they will become virtuous citizens. It is justice, not charity, that is wanting in the world.

equity_note: Wollstonecraft wrote in 1792 — the same year as the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen — deliberately drawing on the Revolution's logic to demand its extension to women. She was ridiculed in her lifetime. Her argument that women 'appear' inferior because they lack education (not because they are inferior) is a sophisticated structural argument that anticipates modern thinking about systemic disadvantage. They will even take away our name.  Consider what value, what meaning is enclosed even in the smallest of our daily habits, in the hundred possessions which even the poorest beggar owns: a handkerchief, an old letter, the photo of a cherished person. These things are part of us, almost like limbs of our body. equity_note: Levi's account is one of the most philosophically precise analyses of dehumanization ever written. equity_note: The Maryland Toleration Act is one of the earliest colonial laws protecting religious freedom — but it only applied to Christians. Jews, atheists, and non-Christians were explicitly excluded, and blasphemy remained a capital offense. The exhaustive list of denominations it protected reveals the religious diversity of colonial Maryland and the real tensions that made this law necessary. title: Common Sense — On the Absurdity of Island Rule Over a Continent
author: Thomas Paine
excerpt: Small islands not capable of protecting themselves, are the proper objects for kingdoms to take under their care; but there is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island. In no instance hath nature made the satellite larger than its primary planet, and as England and America, with respect to each other, reverses the common order of nature, it is evident that they belong to different systems: England to Europe, America to itself.  Europe, and not England, is the parent country of America. This new world hath been the asylum for the persecuted lovers of civil and religious liberty from every part of Europe. Hither have they fled, not from the tender embraces of the mother, but from the cruelty of the monster; and it is so far true of England, that the same tyranny which drove the first emigrants from home, pursues their descendants still.

equity_note: Paine was a recent immigrant and working-class pamphleteer — his voice is distinct from wealthy landowner Founders. Common Sense sold an estimated 500,000 copies in six months. Used in your US.04 End of Unit Assessment Q3-5. The 'satellite/planet' metaphor translates political arguments into natural law — HTS-2: what does using nature as an argument accomplish for Paine's audience? title: George Washington's Farewell Address — On Foreign Entanglements

Hence she must be engaged in frequent controversies, the causes of which are essentially foreign to our concerns. Hence, therefore, it must be unwise in us to implicate ourselves by artificial ties in the ordinary vicissitudes of her politics or the ordinary combinations and collisions of her friendships or enmities.  Our detached and distant situation invites and enables us to pursue a different course. If we remain one people, under an efficient government, the period is not far off when we may defy material injury from external

title: Harriet Hanson Robinson — Early Factory Labor in New England
author: Harriet Hanson Robinson
excerpt: We can hardly realize what a change the cotton factory made in the status of the working women. Hitherto woman had always been a money saving rather than a money earning, member of the community. Her labor could command but small return. If she worked out as servant, or help, her wages were from 50 cents to $1.00 a week; or, if she went from house to house by the day to spin and weave, or do tailoress work, she could get but 75 cents a week and her meals.  As late as 1840 there were only seven vocations outside the home into which the women of New England had entered. At this time woman had no property rights. A widow could be left without her share of her husband's (or the family) property, an incumbrance to his estate.  With their wages they were for the first time in their lives possessed of money, their own money — money they had earned and could spend as they chose; and the mills we
topic: Lowell mills, women's labor, economic independence, market revolution, women's rights
standards: APUSH P4; APUSH P5; NYS 11.3; HTS-2; HTS-3

Available through Fordham Internet Modern History Sourcebooks and the Massachusetts State Library. Used in US.04 End of Unit Assessment Q12-13, New Visions for Public Schools.
equity_note: Robinson worked in the Lowell mills from age 10 and later became an author and suffragist. Her account captures the genuine liberation that factory wages represented for women who had previously had no independent income — while other sources (the labor petition, the factory regulations) show the exploitation that accompanied that liberation. This tension is the core of your US.04 Q12-13. The phrase 'money they had earned and could spend as they chose' is remarkable for its specificity — this is financial autonomy as experienced, not theorized.

title: Letter from Sally Rice — Mill Girl to Her Parents
author: Sally Rice, mill worker
excerpt: I am most 19 years old. I must of course have something of my own before many more years have passed. And where is that something coming from if I go home and earn nothing?  You may think me unkind, but how can you blame me for wanting to stay here? I have but one life to live and I want to enjoy myself as well as I can while I am young. I feel that I am among strangers — away from home and friends, it is rather trying at times — but since I have got the hang of things and have good boardingmates I shall not be unhappy.  I am going to work in the mill and I think I shall like it well enough. I expect to be homesick a good deal at first, but once I am busy I shall not think of it so much. I intend to go into the mill and work till I have got me some clothes and other things that I need.
topic: Lowell mills, young women workers, economic independence, family expectations, agency
standards: APUSH P4; NYS 11.3; HTS-2; K–8 Grade 7-8

equity_note: Sally Rice's letter is one of the most direct expressions of young women's desire for economic independence in the historical record. Her phrase 'I have but one life to live and I want to enjoy myself' is startlingly modern. She is 19, homesick, but determined. Accessible to all grade levels. Used in your US.04 End of Unit Assessment Q12-13. title: Declaration of Sentiments — Seneca Falls Convention

He has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns.
