attribution: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (Reply to Sister Philothea), 1691. Translated in Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz: Poems, Protest, and a Dream (1997). Penguin Classics.
equity_note: Sor Juana was ordered by the Bishop of Puebla to stop her intellectual work and devote herself to religious devotion. Her Reply is one of the most powerful defenses of women's right to education in Western history — written by a nun in colonial Mexico, to a bishop, in 1691. Two years later, she surrendered all her books and scientific instruments. She died the following year during a plague, nursing sick sisters. Ask: what forms of coercion existed in 1691 that could silence a brilliant woman without killing her outright?
systems_addressed: heteropatriarchy; religious persecution; sexism; colonialism

title: Olaudah Equiano — The Interesting Narrative (on the Middle Passage)
author: Olaudah Equiano
excerpt: The first object which saluted my eyes when I arrived on the coast was the sea, and a slave ship which was then riding at anchor and waiting for its cargo. These filled me with astonishment, which was soon converted into terror when I was carried on board. I was immediately handled and tossed up to see if I were sound by some of the crew; and I was now persuaded that I had gotten into a world of bad spirits, and that they were going to kill me.
topic: Transatlantic slave trade, Middle Passage, abolition, Black resistance, self-determination
standards: APW U4; APUSH P2; NYS 11.2; Global II
attribution: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African (1789). Published by the author, London.
equity_note: Equiano wrote this narrative to persuade white British readers to support abolition — which means he had to translate his experience into terms that would make sense to people who had never been enslaved. The book is also controversial: some historians argue he was born in South Carolina, not West Africa, and constructed his African birth to make the abolitionist case stronger. Ask: if that is true, what does it tell us about whose testimony gets believed, and what forms of evidence formerly enslaved people needed to produce to be taken seriously?
systems_addressed: slavery; white supremacy; anti-Blackness; capitalism; imperialism

title: Mary Prince — The History of Mary Prince, A West Indian Slave
author: Mary Prince
excerpt: I have been a slave — I have felt what a slave feels, and I know what a slave knows; and I would have all the good people in England to know it too, that they may break our chains, and set us free.
topic: Slavery, Caribbean, British Empire, women's resistance, abolition
standards: APW U5; APUSH P3; NYS 11.2; Global II
attribution: Mary Prince, The History of Mary Prince, A West Indian Slave (1831). Published by F. Westley and A.H. Davis, London.
equity_note: Mary Prince was the first Black British woman to publish an autobiography. Her account was dictated and transcribed by a white abolitionist editor — which means the text is mediated and possibly shaped for its audience. The slaveholder she named sued for libel and the case revealed how difficult it was to legally challenge slavery through testimony. She was also unable to return to Antigua to be with her husband because she would have been re-enslaved. Ask: how do we read a testimony that was filtered through an editor with their own agenda? What might be missing?
systems_addressed: slavery; white supremacy; anti-Blackness; heteropatriarchy; imperialism

title: José Martí — 'Our America' (on Latin American identity and US imperialism)
author: José Martí
excerpt: The European university must yield to the American university. The history of America, from the Incas to the present, must be taught in clear detail and to the letter, even if the archons of Greece are overlooked. Our Greece must take priority over the Greece which is not ours.
topic: Latin American independence, US imperialism, anti-colonialism, national identity, mestizaje
standards: APW U6; APUSH P6; NYS 10.4; Global II
attribution: José Martí, 'Nuestra América' (Our America), La Revista Ilustrada de Nueva York, January 10, 1891. Translated in José Martí: Selected Writings, Esther Allen, ed. (2002). Penguin Classics.
equity_note: Martí wrote 'Our America' while living in exile in New York, warning Latin American nations that the United States was their greatest threat — not Europe. He was killed in Cuba's independence war in 1895. His essay predates by decades the formal Monroe Doctrine expansion he was warning about, and his concept of 'nuestra América' (our America) claims the name 'America' back from the United States. Ask: whose hemisphere is 'America'? What does it mean that the US has claimed the entire continent's name as its own?
systems_addressed: imperialism; colonialism; white supremacy; nationalism; settler colonialism

title: Ida B. Wells-Barnett — 'Lynch Law in America'
author: Ida B. Wells-Barnett
excerpt: Our country's national crime is lynching. It is not the creature of an hour, the sudden outburst of uncontrolled fury, or the unspeakable brutality of an insane mob. It represents the cool, calculating deliberation of intelligent people who openly avow that there is an 'unwritten law' that justifies them in putting human beings to death without complaint under oath, without trial by jury, without opportunity to make defense.
topic: Lynching, racial terror, white supremacy, anti-Blackness, Jim Crow
attribution: Ida B. Wells-Barnett, 'Lynch Law in America,' The Arena, January 1900. Reprinted in Mildred Thompson, Ida B. Wells-Barnett: An Exploratory Study of an American Black Woman (1990). Carlson Publishing.
equity_note: Wells-Barnett was run out of Memphis with death threats after writing that lynchings were not about protecting white women — as claimed — but about economic and political terror against Black people who were becoming too prosperous or powerful. She had to write this in 1900 for a white magazine to reach white readers. She was also excluded from the founding of the NAACP despite being its intellectual progenitor. Ask: what does it mean when the person who builds an institution doesn't get to lead it? How does that happen, and why?
systems_addressed: white supremacy; anti-Blackness; carceral state; police violence; racial terror

title: Frantz Fanon — The Wretched of the Earth (Preface / on colonial violence)
author: Frantz Fanon
excerpt: Colonialism is not a thinking machine, nor a body endowed with reasoning faculties. It is violence in its natural state, and it will only yield when confronted with greater violence.
topic: Anti-colonialism, Algerian independence, decolonization, racial violence, psychiatry
standards: APW U8; NYS 10.6; Global II; APUSH P8
attribution: Frantz Fanon, Les Damnés de la Terre (The Wretched of the Earth), 1961. Translated by Richard Philcox (2004). Grove Press.
equity_note: Fanon was a psychiatrist who treated both French soldiers and Algerian freedom fighters for trauma — and concluded that colonialism itself was a form of psychological violence that produced mental illness. He wrote The Wretched of the Earth while dying of leukemia at 36. The book was banned in France and seized at borders. It became one of the most influential texts of the 20th century anti-colonial movement and influenced everyone from the Black Panthers to Nelson Mandela. Ask: what kind of knowledge about violence can only be produced from inside the experience of it?
systems_addressed: colonialism; white supremacy; anti-Blackness; imperialism; capitalism; settler colonialism

title: Simone de Beauvoir — The Second Sex (Introduction: 'Woman as Other')
author: Simone de Beauvoir
excerpt: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. No biological, psychological, or economic fate determines the figure that the human female presents in society; it is civilization as a whole that produces this creature, intermediate between male and eunuch, which is described as feminine.
topic: Gender, existentialism, heteropatriarchy, women's liberation, philosophy
standards: APW U7; NYS 10.5; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Simone de Beauvoir, Le Deuxième Sexe (The Second Sex), 1949. Translated by Constance Borde and Sheila Malovany-Chevallier (2010). Knopf.
equity_note: De Beauvoir's 'one is not born a woman, but becomes one' — published in 1949 — is the foundational statement of gender as social construction rather than biological destiny. The book was immediately condemned by the Vatican and placed on the Index of Forbidden Books. Her personal relationship with Sartre, in which she arguably subordinated her career to his, is itself a case study in the structures she was theorizing. Ask: what does it mean to articulate a theory of women's oppression while living within it? Does it change how we read the theory?
systems_addressed: heteropatriarchy; sexism; misogyny; class exploitation

title: Patrice Lumumba — Speech at Congolese Independence Ceremony
author: Patrice Lumumba
excerpt: We are no longer your monkeys… Who will forget the rifle-fire from which so many of our brothers died, or the jails where all those were brutally flung who did not want to submit to a regime of oppression and exploitation — a regime which the colonialists maintained by force?
topic: Congolese independence, anti-colonialism, Belgian Congo, Pan-Africanism
attribution: Patrice Lumumba, speech at Congolese independence ceremony, Léopoldville, June 30, 1960. Translated in Patrice Lumumba, The Truth About a Monstrous Crime of the Colonialists (1961). Foreign Languages Publishing House, Moscow.
equity_note: Lumumba gave this speech directly to the Belgian king's face at the independence ceremony — breaking protocol that called for gratitude toward Belgium. He was assassinated seven months later with CIA and Belgian involvement, a fact declassified in 2001. The CIA station chief in Leopoldville received a personal commendation from the director. Ask: when we say a country gained 'independence,' what does that mean if the first leader who tried to exercise it was killed by the country that granted it?
systems_addressed: colonialism; white supremacy; anti-Blackness; imperialism; capitalism

title: Sylvia Pankhurst — 'Votes for Women' (on militancy and working-class women)
author: Sylvia Pankhurst
excerpt: We are fighting not only for the vote for women, but for the freedom of the whole working class. We want women to have the vote not as a gift from men who will keep all other power in their hands, but as a right of free citizens.
topic: Women's suffrage, class, suffragette movement, working-class women, militancy
attribution: Sylvia Pankhurst, The Suffragette Movement: An Intimate Account of Persons and Ideals (1931), Ch. 22. Longmans, Green and Co.
equity_note: Sylvia Pankhurst broke with her mother Emmeline and sister Christabel over class — they wanted votes for middle-class women through respectable channels; she wanted votes for all women through working-class organizing. The WSPU expelled her. The mainstream suffragette movement largely excluded Black and working-class women. Ask: when a movement achieves its goal for some members by excluding others, what kind of victory is that? Compare to the 15th Amendment and the splits it caused in the women's suffrage movement in the US.
systems_addressed: heteropatriarchy; sexism; class exploitation; capitalism

title: Eduardo Galeano — Open Veins of Latin America (Introduction)
author: Eduardo Galeano
excerpt: The history of Latin America is the history of continuous and underdevelopment. The poverty of Latin America is not a starting point; it is the result. Latin America's underdevelopment is not a stage on the road to development; it is the consequence of development elsewhere.
topic: Latin American history, imperialism, neocolonialism, extractive capitalism, poverty
attribution: Eduardo Galeano, Las venas abiertas de América Latina (Open Veins of Latin America), 1971. Translated by Cedric Belfrage (1973). Monthly Review Press.
equity_note: This book was banned by the military dictatorships of Uruguay, Argentina, and Chile (all US-backed regimes) immediately after publication. Hugo Chávez famously gave a copy to Barack Obama at a 2009 summit. Galeano later said he couldn't reread it — he felt the writing was too 'certain' in ways that troubled him. Ask: what does it mean to write political history with passion and certainty? Does passionate certainty make a book more or less useful as a historical source? Compare to how 'objective' history is taught.
systems_addressed: imperialism; capitalism; neocolonialism; class exploitation; white supremacy

title: Aung San Suu Kyi — Freedom from Fear (Nobel Peace Prize lecture, delivered by proxy)
author: Aung San Suu Kyi
excerpt: It is not power that corrupts but fear. Fear of losing power corrupts those who wield it and fear of the scourge of power corrupts those who are subject to it.
topic: Myanmar, democracy, authoritarianism, nonviolent resistance, human rights
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Aung San Suu Kyi, 'Freedom from Fear,' Nobel Peace Prize lecture, delivered by her son Alexander Aris, Oslo, December 10, 1991. Reprinted in Aung San Suu Kyi, Freedom from Fear and Other Writings (1991). Viking.
equity_note: This source requires a critical discussion of moral complexity: Aung San Suu Kyi spent 15 years under house arrest and won the Nobel Peace Prize as a symbol of democratic resistance — then, as State Counsellor of Myanmar from 2016, refused to condemn or acknowledge the military's genocide of Rohingya Muslims that killed over 10,000 people and displaced 700,000. Ask: can someone be both a genuine victim of authoritarianism AND a perpetuator of genocide against another group? What do we do with the moral complexity of people we once treated as symbols? This is one of the most important contemporary examples of how resistance to one form of oppression does not guarantee resistance to all forms.
systems_addressed: authoritarianism; nationalism; surveillance; imperialism

title: Kimberlé Crenshaw — 'Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex'
author: Kimberlé Crenshaw
excerpt: Black women are sometimes excluded from feminist theory and antiracist policy discourse because both are predicated on a discrete set of experiences that often does not accurately reflect the interaction of race and gender. These problems of exclusion cannot be solved simply by including Black women within an already established analytical structure.
topic: Intersectionality, Black women, anti-discrimination law, race, gender, legal theory
standards: APUSH P9; NYS 12.C3; APW U9; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Kimberlé Crenshaw, 'Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex: A Black Feminist Critique of Antidiscrimination Doctrine, Feminist Theory and Antiracist Politics,' University of Chicago Legal Forum, vol. 1989, no. 1 (1989).
equity_note: Crenshaw coined 'intersectionality' in this 1989 paper to explain a specific legal problem: Black women suing General Motors for discrimination didn't fit into either the 'race discrimination' or 'sex discrimination' legal categories, because the company hired Black men (for factory work) and white women (for office work) — just not Black women. The concept has since become the center of culture war debates, often stripped of its legal origins. Ask: what happens when a precise legal concept becomes a political buzzword? What is lost and what is gained in that translation?
systems_addressed: white supremacy; anti-Blackness; heteropatriarchy; sexism; class exploitation

title: Berta Cáceres — Speech accepting the Goldman Environmental Prize
author: Berta Cáceres
excerpt: Our Mother Earth — militarized, fenced-in, poisoned, a place where basic rights are systematically violated — demands that we take action. Let us come together and remain hopeful as we defend and care for the blood of the Earth and of its spirits.
topic: Indigenous land rights, environmental justice, Honduras, corporate power, femicide
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; Global II Enduring Issues; APUSH P9
attribution: Berta Cáceres, Goldman Environmental Prize acceptance speech, San Francisco, April 20, 2015. Transcript at goldmanprize.org.
equity_note: Cáceres received the Goldman Prize in April 2015 for stopping a dam on the sacred Gualcarque River. She was assassinated in her home in March 2016. The dam was funded by a Dutch development bank and built by a Honduran company with ties to the military. Seven company employees were convicted; in 2021 the CEO was also convicted. She had received over 33 threats and requests for protection that were ignored. Ask: what does it mean that environmental activists — disproportionately Indigenous women — are the most assassinated group of activists in the world? What systems produce that pattern?
systems_addressed: settler colonialism; anti-Indigenous racism; environmental racism; capitalism; neocolonialism

title: James Baldwin — 'A Talk to Teachers'
author: James Baldwin
excerpt: The purpose of education, finally, is to create in a person the ability to look at the world for himself, to make his own decisions, to say to himself this is black or this is white, to decide for himself whether there is a God in heaven or not… But no society is really anxious to have that kind of person around. What societies really, ideally, want is a citizenry which will simply obey the rules of society.
topic: Education, white supremacy, anti-Blackness, democracy, teaching as resistance
attribution: James Baldwin, 'A Talk to Teachers,' Saturday Review, December 21, 1963. Originally delivered as 'The Negro Child — His Self Image,' October 16, 1963.
equity_note: Baldwin gave this speech to teachers in 1963 — the same year as the March on Washington, the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing, and the assassination of Medgar Evers. He is arguing directly to educators that the American education system is designed to produce compliant citizens, not free thinkers — and that this is especially lethal for Black children who must simultaneously learn that system and see through it to survive. This is one of the most powerful texts on the purpose of education ever written. Ask: what is school for? Baldwin's answer, and the system's answer, are not the same.
systems_addressed: white supremacy; anti-Blackness; surveillance; authoritarianism; class exploitation

title: N. Scott Momaday — House Made of Dawn (Prologue excerpt) / Pulitzer acceptance
author: N. Scott Momaday
excerpt: There was a house made of dawn. It was made of pollen and of rain, and the land was very old and everlasting. There were many colors on the hills, and the plain was bright with different-colored clays and sands.
topic: Indigenous literature, Kiowa, Native American identity, cultural survival, settler colonialism
standards: APUSH P8; NYS 11.7; Grade 8 SS; APW U8
attribution: N. Scott Momaday, House Made of Dawn (1968), Prologue. Harper & Row. Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, 1969.
equity_note: Momaday was the first Native American to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, in 1969 — the same year as the occupation of Alcatraz by the American Indian Movement. House Made of Dawn is about a Pueblo veteran returning from World War II who cannot reintegrate because the United States wants his military service but not his Indigeneity. The novel is written in a form that mirrors Kiowa oral storytelling — which means white reviewers initially found it 'difficult' because they didn't recognize the structure. Ask: whose literary traditions define what 'good writing' looks like? What do we call literature that doesn't follow those conventions?
systems_addressed: settler colonialism; anti-Indigenous racism; cultural genocide; white supremacy

title: Audre Lorde — 'The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House'
author: Audre Lorde
excerpt: It is a particular academic arrogance to assume any discussion of feminist theory without examining our many differences, and without a significant input from poor women, Black and Third World women, and lesbians. And yet, I stand here as a Black lesbian feminist, having been invited to comment within the only panel at this conference where the input of Black feminists and lesbians is represented.
topic: Intersectionality, feminism, anti-Blackness, heteropatriarchy, homophobia, difference
standards: APUSH P9; NYS 12.C3; APW U9; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Audre Lorde, 'The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House,' remarks at 'The Personal and the Political Panel,' Second Sex Conference, New York, September 29, 1979. Published in Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (1984). Crossing Press.
equity_note: Lorde delivered this speech at a feminist conference that had invited her to speak on a panel about Black women and lesbians — the only panel with that focus — while the rest of the conference theorized about women in general (meaning white women). The speech is a direct confrontation of white feminism's structural reproduction of the racism it claims to oppose. The title has become shorthand for the argument that you cannot use the logic and methods of an oppressive system to dismantle that system. Ask: what would it look like to use entirely different tools? Can you identify examples in history where people tried to do exactly that?
systems_addressed: white supremacy; anti-Blackness; heteropatriarchy; homophobia; class exploitation; sexism

title: Ed Roberts — Speech at the Independent Living Movement Founding
author: Ed Roberts
excerpt: We are the experts on our own lives. Rehabilitation professionals told me I would never live independently, never go to college, never work. They were wrong about all three. The problem is not our disabilities. The problem is a society that refuses to accommodate us.
topic: Disability rights, Independent Living Movement, ableism, self-determination, civil rights
attribution: Ed Roberts, remarks at the founding of the Center for Independent Living, Berkeley, California, 1972. Archived in Paul K. Longmore Institute on Disability, San Francisco State University.
equity_note: Ed Roberts was told by the California Department of Rehabilitation that he was 'too disabled' to be employable and denied funding — then became Director of that same department. He founded the Independent Living Movement on the principle that disabled people, not rehabilitation professionals, are the experts on disabled lives. The ILM directly parallels civil rights and feminist movements in asserting that the problem is not the person but the structure. Ask: what does it mean to locate the problem in society rather than in the individual? How does that framing change what counts as a solution?
systems_addressed: ableism; sanism; capitalism; class exploitation

title: Harriet McBryde Johnson — 'Unspeakable Conversations' (debate with Peter Singer)
author: Harriet McBryde Johnson
excerpt: He insists he doesn't want to kill me. He simply thinks it would have been better, all things considered, to have given my parents the option of killing the baby I once was, and that it would be better for a baby like I was to be killed. I tell him I agree with him that a life worth living is not one of pure pleasure. But I'm not so sure that I, in particular, have a life not worth living.
topic: Disability rights, bioethics, ableism, quality of life, Peter Singer, right to live
attribution: Harriet McBryde Johnson, 'Unspeakable Conversations,' The New York Times Magazine, February 16, 2003.
equity_note: Johnson, a disability rights lawyer with a progressive neuromuscular disease, was invited to debate philosopher Peter Singer at Princeton — Singer argues that parents should be able to euthanize disabled infants because disability means lower quality of life. Her account of preparing for and surviving this debate is one of the most powerful pieces of disability rights writing in existence. Ask: who gets to determine whether a life is worth living? What assumptions about disability are embedded in Singer's argument — and in our medical, legal, and insurance systems?
systems_addressed: ableism; sanism; capitalism; class exploitation

title: Marsha P. Johnson — 'I Got My Tips from the Stonewall' (interview)
author: Marsha P. Johnson
excerpt: I was no one, nobody, from Nowheresville until I became a drag queen. That's what started my career — being a drag queen… Darling, I want to be remembered as a person who fought for gay liberation and all the oppressed people that needed to be fought for.
topic: Stonewall, LGBTQ+ rights, trans history, queer resistance, police violence, homelessness
attribution: Marsha P. Johnson, interview with Eric Marcus, Making Gay History oral history project, New York City, 1992. Archived at makinggayhistory.com.
equity_note: Marsha P. Johnson was a Black trans woman who was present at Stonewall in 1969 — one of the people who threw the first objects at police. She is often described as 'throwing the first brick' though she disputed that specific detail. She co-founded STAR (Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries) with Sylvia Rivera, providing shelter for homeless trans youth. Her body was found in the Hudson River in 1992; police ruled it a suicide; activists disputed this for decades. Ask: the mainstream LGBTQ+ rights movement has centered white, gay, cisgender men since the 1970s. What does it mean that the people most responsible for Stonewall were Black trans women who remained houseless and marginalized?
systems_addressed: homophobia; transphobia; anti-Blackness; white supremacy; carceral state; police violence

title: Bayard Rustin — 'The New Niggers Are Gays' (speech)
author: Bayard Rustin
excerpt: The only real coalition we can make is a coalition of those who are at the bottom — the most despised people of this society, those who are poor, those who are Black, those who are gay. Unless we build that coalition, we will not move forward.
topic: Civil rights, LGBTQ+ rights, anti-Blackness, homophobia, intersectionality, HIV/AIDS
attribution: Bayard Rustin, 'The New Niggers Are Gays,' speech at a New York LGBTQ+ rights forum, 1986. Reprinted in Walter Naegle, ed., Time on Two Crosses: The Collected Writings of Bayard Rustin (2003). Cleis Press.
equity_note: Bayard Rustin organized the 1963 March on Washington — including the logistics of moving 250,000 people — and was the primary strategist behind Martin Luther King Jr.'s commitment to nonviolence. He was kept in the background of the civil rights movement because he was openly gay. King's advisors told him Rustin's homosexuality would be used against the movement. Rustin came out publicly in 1986, near the end of his life, as the HIV/AIDS epidemic decimated the LGBTQ+ community. Ask: what does it mean when a movement's most essential organizer is hidden because of who he is? What was lost by hiding him?
systems_addressed: homophobia; anti-Blackness; white supremacy; class exploitation; carceral state

title: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta — United Farm Workers Founding (joint statement)
author: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta
excerpt: We have been farm workers for hundreds of years and pioneers who helped make this country rich. While this continues, we are still pilgrims on this planet. We shall not endure. Strike!
topic: Labor rights, Chicano movement, farmworkers, racism, capitalism, nonviolent resistance
attribution: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta, statement at the founding of the United Farm Workers strike, Delano, California, September 16, 1965. UFW archives; reprinted in Jacques Levy, Cesar Chavez: Autobiography of La Causa (1975). Norton.
equity_note: The Delano grape strike began on Mexican Independence Day — a deliberate choice. Dolores Huerta co-founded the UFW and coined 'Sí, se puede' (Yes, we can) — the phrase later adopted by Barack Obama's campaign. She is often erased from the history in favor of Chavez alone. The strike lasted five years and ended when major California growers signed contracts. Ask: the labor movement has repeatedly excluded or marginalized workers of color. What does it mean when the people who built American agriculture are also the people most excluded from its protections?
systems_addressed: capitalism; labor exploitation; anti-Latino racism; class exploitation; white supremacy

title: Wangari Maathai — Nobel Peace Prize Acceptance Speech
author: Wangari Maathai
excerpt: Today we are faced with a challenge that calls for a shift in our thinking, so that humanity stops threatening its life-support system. We are called to assist the Earth to heal her wounds and in the process heal our own — indeed, to embrace the whole of creation in all its diversity, beauty and wonder.
topic: Environmental justice, democracy, women's rights, Kenya, colonialism, Green Belt Movement
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Wangari Maathai, Nobel Peace Prize acceptance speech, Oslo, Norway, December 10, 2004. Nobel Foundation archives at nobelprize.org.
equity_note: Maathai was the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize — for planting trees. The Green Belt Movement she founded planted over 51 million trees across Kenya while simultaneously organizing women against the Moi dictatorship. She was beaten by police at her own tree-planting ceremonies. She connected deforestation to colonialism, poverty, and women's disempowerment as a single linked system — not separate issues. Ask: why was the Nobel Peace Prize given for planting trees? What theory of peace does that reflect? Compare to who typically wins the prize.
systems_addressed: environmental racism; colonialism; heteropatriarchy; authoritarianism; capitalism

title: Edward Said — 'Zionism from the Standpoint of Its Victims'
author: Edward Said
excerpt: Zionism saw Palestine as the site of its colonial project, and it was so successful in this that it effectively screened out the indigenous Palestinian reality, first through the philanthropic myth of 'a land without a people for a people without a land,' and then through the military and political power of the Israeli state.
topic: Palestine, Zionism, settler colonialism, imperialism, Orientalism, displacement
standards: APW U8; APW U9; NYS 10.6; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Edward Said, 'Zionism from the Standpoint of Its Victims,' Social Text, no. 1 (Winter 1979). Duke University Press.
equity_note: Said wrote this as a counter-narrative to dominant Western accounts that presented Zionism as a straightforward liberation movement — applying the same settler-colonial framework used to analyze the Americas and South Africa to Israel/Palestine. This source requires careful pedagogical framing: it is a legitimate scholarly argument by a major intellectual, not propaganda. Students should also read pro-Zionist arguments. Ask: what does it mean to apply the same analytical framework to all settler-colonial situations? Does consistency require that we either condemn all of them or find different criteria for some?
systems_addressed: settler colonialism; imperialism; anti-Indigenous racism; nationalism; Islamophobia

title: B.R. Ambedkar — Annihilation of Caste (excerpt)
author: B.R. Ambedkar
excerpt: You are asking me to address the Conference of Social Reform. But I am sorry to say that I cannot look upon the movement for Social Reform in the way in which it is being carried on today as anything but a snare and a delusion… Caste cannot be just reformed. It must be annihilated.
topic: Caste, Hinduism, untouchability, Dalit rights, India, structural racism, social justice
standards: APW U6; APW U7; NYS 10.3; Global II
attribution: B.R. Ambedkar, Annihilation of Caste, 1936 (written as a speech; organizers canceled the event after reading it). Published independently by Ambedkar. Annotated edition by Arundhati Roy (2014). Verso.
equity_note: Ambedkar wrote this speech for a Hindu caste reform conference — and the organizers canceled the conference rather than let him give it. He published it himself. He is to Dalit liberation what Frederick Douglass is to Black liberation in the United States — and is almost completely absent from American K-12 curriculum. He also wrote the Indian Constitution. Arundhati Roy's 2014 annotated edition connects his arguments to contemporary India. Ask: what does it mean that the man who wrote India's constitution was a member of the caste that could not enter temples, draw water from public wells, or walk on public roads?
systems_addressed: caste; class exploitation; religious persecution; white supremacy; heteropatriarchy

title: Qiu Jin — 'An Address to Two Hundred Million Fellow Countrywomen'
author: Qiu Jin
excerpt: Alas, the greatest injustice in the world must be that of our two hundred million women. Since we were born, what crimes have we committed that we should be subject to this oppression? We are denied education, we are forbidden to develop our talents, we are not even allowed to go out of the house!
topic: Chinese nationalism, women's liberation, foot binding, imperialism, Qing dynasty, revolution
attribution: Qiu Jin, 'Jingao eryi nü tongbao' (An Address to Two Hundred Million Fellow Countrywomen), Zhongguo nübao (Chinese Women's Journal), 1907. Translated in Patricia Ebrey, Chinese Civilization: A Sourcebook (1993). Free Press.
equity_note: Qiu Jin was beheaded by the Qing government six months after writing this essay, at age 31, for her involvement in a revolutionary plot. She had left her husband and children to go to Japan, study, and join the revolutionary movement. She dressed in men's clothing, fenced, and wrote poetry. She is a national hero in China but almost unknown in American education. Ask: what would the world history curriculum look like if it included women who took up arms for their own liberation alongside men who did the same?
systems_addressed: heteropatriarchy; sexism; imperialism; nationalism

title: Emiliano Zapata — Plan de Ayala (on land and liberty)
author: Emiliano Zapata
excerpt: The lands, woods, and waters that have been usurped by the hacendados, cientificos, or bosses, in the shadow of tyranny and venal justice, will be restored immediately to the villages or citizens who hold the corresponding titles to these properties… The insurgent army of the Revolution will maintain order and will apply, without delay, these agreements.
topic: Mexican Revolution, land reform, Indigenous rights, capitalism, agrarian justice
standards: APW U6; NYS 10.3; Global II; APUSH P6
attribution: Emiliano Zapata, Plan de Ayala, November 28, 1911. Translated in John Womack Jr., Zapata and the Mexican Revolution (1969). Knopf.
equity_note: Zapata's slogan 'Tierra y Libertad' (Land and Liberty) became the rallying cry of Mexico's peasant revolution. The Plan de Ayala demanded that land stolen from Indigenous communities be returned — a demand that anticipated 20th century land reform movements across Latin America. Zapata was assassinated in 1919. His name was adopted by the Zapatista movement (EZLN) in Chiapas in 1994, which launched its uprising the day NAFTA took effect, arguing that free trade was a new form of land dispossession. Ask: why do the same land rights arguments recur across 80 years? What does that tell us about whether the underlying problem was ever resolved?
systems_addressed: capitalism; land dispossession; settler colonialism; class exploitation; anti-Indigenous racism

title: Thomas Sankara — Speech on Women's Liberation in Burkina Faso
author: Thomas Sankara
excerpt: Comrades, there is no true social revolution without the liberation of women. May my eyes never see and my feet never take me to a society where half the people are held in silence. I hear the roar of women's silence. I sense the rumble of their storm and feel the fury of their revolt.
topic: African socialism, women's liberation, colonialism, imperialism, Burkina Faso, intersectionality
attribution: Thomas Sankara, 'The Revolution Cannot Triumph Without the Emancipation of Women,' speech on International Women's Day, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, March 8, 1987. Translated in Thomas Sankara Speaks: The Burkina Faso Revolution 1983-87 (2007). Pathfinder Press.
equity_note: Sankara governed Burkina Faso from 1983-1987 and is called 'Africa's Che Guevara.' His government banned female genital mutilation, forced marriages, and polygamy; recruited women into the military; and launched mass literacy campaigns. He reduced his own salary, flew economy class, and sold the presidential fleet. He was assassinated in a coup in 1987, allegedly with French involvement. Ask: Sankara is almost unknown in American education while being one of the most influential leaders of 20th century Africa. What criteria determine which world leaders become part of the curriculum?
systems_addressed: heteropatriarchy; sexism; colonialism; imperialism; capitalism

title: Idle No More — Manifesto (Indigenous sovereignty in Canada)
author: Idle No More Founders (Sylvia McAdam, Jessica Gordon, Nina Wilson, Sheelah McLean)
excerpt: We contend that colonial and capitalist forces are being imposed on Indigenous peoples, traditional lands and waters. Idle No More calls on all people to join in a peaceful revolution to honor Indigenous sovereignty and to protect the land and water.
topic: Indigenous sovereignty, treaty rights, settler colonialism, Canada, environmental racism
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Idle No More, founding manifesto, December 2012. Published at idlenomore.ca.
equity_note: Idle No More began as four women — three Indigenous, one white ally — organizing against Canadian legislation that weakened environmental protections on Indigenous lands. It grew into one of the largest Indigenous rights movements in Canadian history, with round dances in shopping malls becoming a form of protest. Founded by women, it centered Indigenous women's leadership at a time when Canada was simultaneously experiencing a crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls. Ask: what does it mean when the people most affected by an environmental policy are the same people whose legal protections have just been stripped?
systems_addressed: settler colonialism; anti-Indigenous racism; environmental racism; capitalism; land dispossession

title: Ruha Benjamin — Race After Technology (on the 'New Jim Code')
author: Ruha Benjamin
excerpt: The New Jim Code is the employment of new technologies that reflect and reproduce existing inequities but that are promoted and perceived as more objective or progressive than the discriminatory systems of a previous era.
topic: Algorithmic racism, technology, anti-Blackness, surveillance, capitalism, automation
attribution: Ruha Benjamin, Race After Technology: Abolitionist Tools for the New Jim Code (2019), Ch. 1. Polity Press.
equity_note: Benjamin's concept of the 'New Jim Code' argues that digital technologies don't eliminate racial bias — they encode it into algorithms that appear neutral. Examples include: facial recognition that misidentifies Black faces, predictive policing that concentrates surveillance in Black neighborhoods, healthcare algorithms that systematically underestimate Black patients' pain, and hiring algorithms trained on historically biased data. Ask: what does it mean when a discriminatory system is replaced by an automated one that produces the same results? Is that progress? Pairs directly with Joy Buolamwini's testimony (l018).
systems_addressed: white supremacy; anti-Blackness; surveillance; capitalism; carceral state

title: W.E.B. Du Bois — Black Reconstruction in America (excerpt: 'The Propaganda of History')
author: W.E.B. Du Bois
excerpt: One is astonished in the study of history at the recurrence of the idea that evil must be forgotten, distorted, skimmed over. We must not remember that Daniel Webster got drunk but only remember that he was a splendid constitutional lawyer. We must forget that George Washington was a slave owner… Nations reel and stagger on their way; they make hideous mistakes; they commit frightful wrongs.
topic: Reconstruction, historical memory, white supremacy, anti-Blackness, historiography, Lost Cause
standards: APUSH P5; APUSH P6; NYS 11.4; Grade 8 SS
attribution: W.E.B. Du Bois, Black Reconstruction in America 1860-1880 (1935), Ch. 17: 'The Propaganda of History.' Harcourt, Brace and Company.
equity_note: Du Bois wrote this in 1935 as a direct challenge to the Dunning School of Reconstruction history, which was then the dominant academic account — portraying Reconstruction as a disaster caused by incompetent Black politicians and corrupt Northern carpetbaggers. His version argued that Reconstruction was a genuine democratic revolution, destroyed by white supremacist violence. The Dunning School is the historical framework behind Birth of a Nation (1915) and the Lost Cause mythology. Ask: when historians lie, what are the consequences? Connect to current debates about history curricula and what gets taught in schools.
systems_addressed: white supremacy; anti-Blackness; nationalism; settler colonialism

title: Shirin Ebadi — Nobel Peace Prize Lecture (on women, Islam, and human rights)
author: Shirin Ebadi
excerpt: In the past two decades, despite all the obstacles, I have not lost my faith in justice. I am still committed to democracy, human rights, and the rule of law. I believe that the rights of women can be and must be addressed within an Islamic framework — not by abandoning Islam, but by reinterpreting it.
topic: Iran, women's rights, Islam, human rights, democracy, authoritarianism
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Shirin Ebadi, Nobel Peace Prize lecture, Oslo, Norway, December 10, 2003. Nobel Foundation archives at nobelprize.org.
equity_note: Ebadi was the first Iranian woman and first Muslim woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. The Iranian government responded by airing a TV program that night about a different Nobel laureate. She argues that human rights and Islam are not incompatible — which challenges both Iranian theocracy AND Western Islamophobia simultaneously. She was later stripped of her Nobel medal by Iranian authorities. Ask: what does it mean to argue for women's rights within a religious tradition rather than against it? How is that different from Western secular frameworks for women's rights?
systems_addressed: heteropatriarchy; authoritarianism; Islamophobia; religious persecution; sexism

title: Robert Bullard — 'Anatomy of Environmental Racism and the Environmental Justice Movement'
author: Robert Bullard
excerpt: Blacks and other minorities are exposed to greater environmental threats and health risks than are whites. Blacks are heavily concentrated in areas with the highest levels of air pollution, toxic waste sites, and other environmental hazards. This unequal distribution of environmental burdens is no accident.
topic: Environmental racism, toxic waste, anti-Blackness, environmental justice, capitalism
attribution: Robert Bullard, 'Anatomy of Environmental Racism and the Environmental Justice Movement,' in Confronting Environmental Racism: Voices from the Grassroots, Robert Bullard, ed. (1993). South End Press.
equity_note: Bullard coined the term 'environmental racism' after his wife asked him to study where toxic waste facilities were located in Houston, expecting to find an economic pattern. He found that race — not income — was the primary predictor of proximity to environmental hazards. This research helped launch the environmental justice movement and led directly to an Executive Order on Environmental Justice in 1994. Ask: if you mapped the location of every toxic waste facility, factory farm, and polluted waterway in America, what would the map look like? Why does that pattern exist?
systems_addressed: environmental racism; anti-Blackness; white supremacy; capitalism; class exploitation

title: Kwame Nkrumah — Neocolonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism (Introduction)
author: Kwame Nkrumah
excerpt: The essence of neo-colonialism is that the State which is subject to it is, in theory, independent and has all the outward trappings of international sovereignty. In reality its economic system and thus its political policy is directed from outside.
topic: Neocolonialism, imperialism, African independence, capitalism, Cold War, Pan-Africanism
attribution: Kwame Nkrumah, Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism (1965), Introduction. Thomas Nelson & Sons, London.
equity_note: Nkrumah was the first president of independent Ghana — and was overthrown in a CIA-backed coup in 1966, the year after this book was published. The US State Department's immediate response to the book's publication was to issue a formal protest. Nkrumah's concept of neocolonialism — political independence without economic independence — describes what happened to most formerly colonized nations after formal decolonization: they remained economically dependent on their former colonizers through debt, trade agreements, and military presence. Ask: what does independence mean if the economy is still controlled by outsiders?
systems_addressed: imperialism; neocolonialism; capitalism; anti-Blackness; colonialism

title: Naomi Klein — The Shock Doctrine (excerpt: on disaster capitalism)
author: Naomi Klein
excerpt: I call this tactic the shock doctrine: the orchestrated raids on the public sphere in the wake of catastrophic events, combined with the treatment of disasters as exciting market opportunities. The shock doctrine mimics the treatment used in psychological torture — a sudden, disorientating blow that leaves the victim unable to protect their interests.
topic: Disaster capitalism, neoliberalism, imperialism, US foreign policy, structural adjustment
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; APUSH P9; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Naomi Klein, The Shock Doctrine: The Rise of Disaster Capitalism (2007), Introduction. Metropolitan Books.
equity_note: Klein's central argument is that free-market economic policies — privatization, deregulation, cuts to public services — have historically been implemented not through democratic persuasion but through the disorientation caused by disasters (coups, economic crises, natural disasters, wars). Her examples include post-Pinochet Chile, post-Soviet Russia, post-Katrina New Orleans, and post-invasion Iraq. Ask: if democratic populations consistently reject these policies when asked, but accept them during crises when they can't organize resistance, what does that tell us about the relationship between capitalism and democracy?
systems_addressed: capitalism; neoliberalism; imperialism; authoritarianism; surveillance

title: Arundhati Roy — 'Come September' (on empire and resistance)
author: Arundhati Roy
excerpt: What is the acceptable threshold of [civilian] casualties? Obviously, it depends on who is doing the killing and who is being killed… How many dead Iraqis will it take to make the world a better place? How many dead Afghans? How many dead Palestinians? … There's a lot of counting to be done.
topic: US imperialism, 9/11, War on Terror, corporate power, India, nuclear weapons, resistance
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; APUSH P9; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Arundhati Roy, 'Come September,' lecture at the Lannan Foundation, Santa Fe, New Mexico, September 18, 2002. Published in War Talk (2003). South End Press.
equity_note: Roy gave this speech one year after 9/11, arguing that US foreign policy created the conditions for the attacks, that the War on Terror was a cover for imperial expansion, and that counting only American casualties while dismissing Iraqi and Afghan casualties revealed a hierarchy of human life built into US foreign policy. She received death threats. Ask: is it possible to simultaneously hold that 9/11 was a tragedy AND that the US response killed far more civilians than the attacks themselves? How do we count casualties in a way that treats all human lives equally?
systems_addressed: imperialism; nationalism; white supremacy; capitalism; anti-Muslim racism; Islamophobia

title: Noam Chomsky — Manufacturing Consent (excerpt: on the propaganda model)
author: Noam Chomsky and Edward Herman
excerpt: The mass media serve as a system for communicating messages and symbols to the general populace. It is their function to amuse, entertain, and inform, and to inculcate individuals with the values, beliefs, and codes of behavior that will integrate them into the institutional structures of the larger society. In a world of concentrated wealth and major conflicts of class interest, to fulfill this role requires systematic propaganda.
topic: Media, propaganda, capitalism, democracy, US foreign policy, corporate power
attribution: Noam Chomsky and Edward Herman, Manufacturing Consent: The Political Economy of the Mass Media (1988), Introduction. Pantheon Books.
equity_note: Chomsky and Herman argue that corporate media doesn't engage in overt censorship — it doesn't need to, because journalists are selected and promoted for sharing the values of corporate ownership, and structural filters (advertising dependence, source access, flak from powerful interests) systematically shape which stories get told and how. The argument is empirical, not conspiratorial: they demonstrate it through systematic comparison of how US media covered US-backed atrocities vs. enemy atrocities. Ask: if bias in media is structural rather than intentional, how do you detect it? What would unbiased coverage of US foreign policy look like?
systems_addressed: capitalism; propaganda; surveillance; nationalism; authoritarianism

title: Thucydides — The Melian Dialogue (Athens to Melos: might makes right)
author: Thucydides
excerpt: The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must… You know as well as we do that right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
topic: Imperialism, power, justice, democracy, colonialism, military coercion
standards: APW U1; NYS 9.1; Global II; Grade 6 SS
attribution: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book V, Chapters 84-116 (The Melian Dialogue), ca. 415 BCE. Translated by Richard Crawley (1874); revised translation.
equity_note: Athens demanded that the small island of Melos submit or be destroyed — Melos refused and was annihilated. This dialogue is the clearest articulation of imperial power logic in ancient history: justice is irrelevant between unequal powers. Athens was a democracy. Ask: what does it mean that the world's first democracy simultaneously built an empire through exactly this kind of coercion? How does this challenge the idea that democracy produces more just foreign policy? What contemporary situations does this dialogue describe?
systems_addressed: imperialism; nationalism; capitalism; authoritarianism

title: Cicero — On the Republic (excerpt: on justice and empire)
author: Cicero (Marcus Tullius Cicero)
excerpt: The most foolish notion of all is the belief that everything is just which is found in the customs or laws of nations… What of the many deadly, the many pestilential statutes which nations put in force? These no more deserve to be called laws than the rules a band of robbers might pass in their assembly.
topic: Roman Republic, justice, empire, natural law, civic duty, slavery
standards: APW U1; APW U2; NYS 9.1; Global II; Grade 6 SS
attribution: Cicero, De Re Publica (On the Republic), 54 BCE. Translated by Niall Rudd (1998). Oxford World's Classics.
equity_note: Cicero argues that unjust laws are not laws — a foundational argument later used by abolitionists, civil rights activists, and resistance movements across history. He also owned enslaved people and supported Roman imperial expansion. His natural law argument was simultaneously a critique of tyranny and a defense of Roman imperial order as inherently just. Ask: can the same philosophical framework be used to both defend and critique empire? What does it mean that 'all men are created equal' was written by slaveholders? How do we read arguments for justice made by people who perpetuated injustice?
systems_addressed: imperialism; class exploitation; slavery; nationalism

title: Francis Bacon — Novum Organum (on scientific method and dominion over nature)
author: Francis Bacon
excerpt: Knowledge is power… Nature to be commanded must be obeyed. And that which in contemplation is as the cause, is in operation as the rule… Human knowledge and human power meet in one; for where the cause is not known the effect cannot be produced.
topic: Scientific Revolution, knowledge as power, colonialism, Enlightenment, nature, empire
attribution: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (New Instrument), 1620. Translated in The Works of Francis Bacon, James Spedding et al., eds. (1858). Longman.
equity_note: Bacon's 'knowledge is power' and 'nature to be commanded must be obeyed' are the philosophical foundations of both modern science and extractive capitalism. His framework treats the natural world as a resource to be dominated and controlled — the same logic later applied to colonized peoples. Carolyn Merchant's feminist analysis shows Bacon's scientific writings use metaphors of interrogating nature like interrogating a witch. Ask: what are the consequences of framing human progress as dominion over nature? How does that framework connect to both environmental destruction and colonial extraction?
systems_addressed: imperialism; capitalism; environmental racism; colonialism

title: Michel Foucault — Discipline and Punish (excerpt: the panopticon)
author: Michel Foucault
excerpt: The panoptic mechanism arranges spatial unities that make it possible to see constantly and to recognize immediately… visibility is a trap… He is seen, but he does not see; he is the object of information, never a subject in communication.
topic: Surveillance, carceral state, power, discipline, schools, prisons, modern institutions
standards: APW U9; NYS 12.G5; APUSH P9; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Michel Foucault, Surveiller et Punir: Naissance de la Prison (Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison), 1975. Translated by Alan Sheridan (1977). Pantheon Books.
equity_note: Foucault argues that modern institutions — schools, prisons, hospitals, factories — are all built on the same architecture of surveillance and normalized discipline. The panopticon (a prison design where inmates can never know if they're being watched) becomes a metaphor for how modern power works: not through force but through internalized self-surveillance. Students are disciplined through exactly the mechanisms Foucault describes. Ask: how does your school use surveillance? Who is watched most closely, and who is almost never watched? What behavior does constant surveillance produce?
systems_addressed: carceral state; surveillance; authoritarianism; capitalism; ableism

title: Paul Robeson — Testimony before HUAC (on Black American loyalty and Africa)
author: Paul Robeson
excerpt: My father was a slave, and my people died to build this country, and I am going to stay here, and have a part of it just like you. And no fascist-minded people will drive me from it. Is that clear? I am for peace with the Soviet Union, and I am for peace with China, and I think—
topic: McCarthyism, anti-Blackness, anti-communism, surveillance, civil rights, Africa
attribution: Paul Robeson, testimony before the House Un-American Activities Committee, Washington D.C., June 12, 1956. Congressional Record; reprinted in Philip Foner, ed., Paul Robeson Speaks (1978). Brunner/Mazel.
equity_note: Robeson — opera singer, football All-American, Phi Beta Kappa graduate, and one of the most famous Black Americans of the 20th century — had his passport revoked for eight years for refusing to sign a loyalty oath. He was asked at HUAC why he didn't stay in the Soviet Union if he liked it so much. He responded that his father was a slave and he had as much right to this country as anyone in the room. His career was destroyed. Ask: what is the relationship between Black Americans' demands for civil rights at home and their sympathy for anti-colonial movements abroad? Why did the U.S. government treat those two things as a single threat?
systems_addressed: anti-Blackness; white supremacy; surveillance; carceral state; anti-communism; imperialism

title: Lillian Hellman — Letter to HUAC ('I cannot and will not cut my conscience')
author: Lillian Hellman
excerpt: I am not willing, now or in the future, to bring bad trouble to people who, in my past association with them, were completely innocent of any talk or action that was disloyal or subversive… I cannot and will not cut my conscience to fit this year's fashions.
topic: McCarthyism, free speech, conscience, surveillance, anti-communism, blacklisting
attribution: Lillian Hellman, letter to the House Un-American Activities Committee, May 19, 1952. Reprinted in Lillian Hellman, Scoundrel Time (1976). Little, Brown.
equity_note: Hellman refused to name names before HUAC — taking the Fifth Amendment on questions about herself but refusing to testify about others. 'I cannot and will not cut my conscience to fit this year's fashions' became one of the most quoted lines of resistance to McCarthyism. She was blacklisted. Her partner Dashiell Hammett went to prison. Ask: what is the moral difference between 'I won't answer questions about myself' and 'I won't answer questions about others'? What does it mean to protect others at personal cost? How is this different from the choices made by people who did name names?
systems_addressed: surveillance; authoritarianism; anti-communism; capitalism; nationalism

title: Sukarno — Speech at the Bandung Conference (on non-alignment)
author: Sukarno
excerpt: All of us, I am certain, are united by more important things than those which superficially divide us. We are united, for instance, by a common detestation of colonialism in whatever form it appears. We are united by a common detestation of racialism. And we are united by a common determination to preserve and stabilize peace in the world.
topic: Non-Aligned Movement, decolonization, Cold War, Bandung Conference, Global South solidarity
attribution: Sukarno, opening address at the Asian-African Conference, Bandung, Indonesia, April 18, 1955. Reprinted in George McTurnan Kahin, The Asian-African Conference (1956). Cornell University Press.
equity_note: The Bandung Conference assembled leaders from 29 nations representing over half the world's population — nations that refused to align with either the US or Soviet bloc. It was the founding moment of what became the Non-Aligned Movement. Sukarno called it 'the first intercontinental conference of colored peoples in the history of mankind.' The CIA was deeply alarmed. Ask: why did the existence of a 'third way' between the US and Soviet Union threaten both superpowers? What does it tell us about the Cold War that non-alignment was treated as a threat?
systems_addressed: colonialism; imperialism; white supremacy; nationalism; anti-Blackness

title: Haunani-Kay Trask — 'Lovely Hula Hands: Corporate Tourism and the Prostitution of Hawaiian Culture'
author: Haunani-Kay Trask
excerpt: We are prostituted: our hospitality, our culture, our aloha. We invite you to come and use us. Tourism, then, is not benign… it is the commercialization of our culture and the prostitution of our people.
topic: Hawaiian sovereignty, settler colonialism, tourism, cultural exploitation, Indigenous rights
attribution: Haunani-Kay Trask, 'Lovely Hula Hands: Corporate Tourism and the Prostitution of Hawaiian Culture,' Frontiers: A Journal of Women Studies, vol. 12, no. 1 (1991).
equity_note: Trask was a professor of Hawaiian Studies at UH Mānoa and a leader of the Hawaiian sovereignty movement. She argues that tourism doesn't bring 'aloha' — it extracts it, converting Indigenous culture into a product for white consumers while Native Hawaiians remain dispossessed of their land. Hawaiʻi was illegally annexed by the United States in 1898 through a coup against Queen Liliʻuokalani. The US formally apologized in 1993. Ask: what is the difference between sharing culture and having it commodified without consent? Who profits from Hawaiian 'aloha,' and who owns the land it's sold on?
systems_addressed: settler colonialism; anti-Indigenous racism; capitalism; environmental racism; white supremacy

title: Naguib Mahfouz — Nobel Prize Lecture (on Arabic literature and civilization)
author: Naguib Mahfouz
excerpt: I am the son of two civilizations that at a certain age have melted together in a happy marriage. The first, seven thousand years old, is the Pharaonic civilization; the second, one thousand four hundred years old, is the Islamic civilization… I have lived in this world for only a little more than seventy years, but I have witnessed events that could fill a thousand years of history.
topic: Arabic literature, Egyptian identity, postcolonialism, civilization, cultural dignity
attribution: Naguib Mahfouz, Nobel Prize in Literature acceptance lecture, delivered by proxy, Stockholm, December 8, 1988. Nobel Foundation archives at nobelprize.org.
equity_note: Mahfouz was the first Arabic-language writer to win the Nobel Prize for Literature — in 1988. His Cairo Trilogy is often compared to Dickens and Tolstoy in scope. He was stabbed in the neck in 1994 by Islamist extremists who objected to passages in one of his earlier novels. He survived but lost much of his fine motor control. Ask: what does it mean that the greatest Arab novelist of the 20th century is almost never taught in American schools? What does the literature curriculum reveal about whose stories count as 'universal'?
systems_addressed: imperialism; colonialism; Islamophobia; nationalism

title: Leila Ahmed — Women and Gender in Islam (excerpt: on the colonial discourse on the veil)
author: Leila Ahmed
excerpt: The peculiar practice of Western powers of subordinating women in their own societies while decrying the subordination of women in colonized societies — and using that decrying as a justification for colonialism — is a practice that still continues.
topic: Islam, women's rights, veil, colonialism, Orientalism, feminism, Egypt
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Leila Ahmed, Women and Gender in Islam: Historical Roots of a Modern Debate (1992), Ch. 8. Yale University Press.
equity_note: Ahmed demonstrates that British colonialists in Egypt who argued that Islam oppressed women simultaneously opposed women's suffrage at home — Lord Cromer, who lectured Egyptians about the veil, founded the Men's League for Opposing Women's Suffrage in Britain. The 'save Muslim women' argument has been used to justify every Western military intervention in the Muslim world from Algeria to Afghanistan. Ask: what does it mean when the same governments that deny women rights at home use women's rights abroad as a justification for war? Who defines what 'women's liberation' means, and for whose benefit?
systems_addressed: Islamophobia; imperialism; heteropatriarchy; colonialism; white supremacy

title: Adam Smith — The Wealth of Nations (excerpt: on the division of labor and self-interest)
author: Adam Smith
excerpt: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own self-interest. We address ourselves, not to their humanity but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities but of their advantages.
topic: Capitalism, free market, division of labor, self-interest, economic theory
standards: APW U5; NYS 10.2; Global II; APUSH P3
attribution: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Ch. 1-2. Strahan and Cadell, London.
equity_note: Smith's 'invisible hand' became the foundational argument for free-market capitalism — the idea that individual self-interest, aggregated through markets, produces social benefit. Published the same year as the Declaration of Independence, it provided the economic philosophy for modern capitalism. What is rarely taught: Smith also warned against monopolies, criticized merchants who fixed prices against the public interest, and wrote sympathetically about workers. The version of Smith taught in economics class is much simpler than the actual text. Ask: what gets selected from a foundational text, and what gets left out? Pairs with Marx, Engels, and Galeano.
systems_addressed: capitalism; class exploitation; labor exploitation; imperialism

title: John Locke — Second Treatise of Government (on property and natural rights)
author: John Locke
excerpt: Though the earth, and all inferior creatures, be common to all men, yet every man has a property in his own person: this no body has any right to but himself. The labour of his body, and the work of his hands, we may say, are properly his.
topic: Natural rights, property, democracy, colonialism, settler colonialism, Enlightenment
standards: APW U4; APW U5; NYS 10.1; Global II; APUSH P2
attribution: John Locke, Two Treatises of Government, Second Treatise (1689), Ch. 5. Published 1690.
equity_note: Locke's theory of property — that labor mixed with land creates ownership — is both the foundation of liberal democracy and the philosophical justification for colonialism: Indigenous peoples who didn't 'improve' land through European-style agriculture were deemed not to own it. Locke was an investor in the Royal African Company, which transported enslaved Africans, and helped write the constitution for the Carolina colony. Ask: what does it mean that the founding philosophy of 'natural rights' and 'self-ownership' was written by a man who invested in the slave trade? How does that contradiction live inside the documents built on his ideas?
systems_addressed: settler colonialism; capitalism; anti-Indigenous racism; class exploitation; heteropatriarchy

title: Winston Churchill — 'We Shall Fight on the Beaches' speech
author: Winston Churchill
excerpt: We shall fight on the seas and oceans, we shall fight with growing confidence and growing strength in the air, we shall defend our island, whatever the cost may be, we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall never surrender.
topic: WWII, British imperialism, nationalism, war rhetoric, Dunkirk, colonialism
attribution: Winston Churchill, speech to the House of Commons, London, June 4, 1940. Hansard, vol. 361, cols. 787-796.
equity_note: Churchill's speech is one of the most celebrated examples of wartime rhetoric in English. It is less often taught that the same Churchill oversaw a famine in Bengal in 1943 that killed between 2 and 3 million people, blocked food relief, and said Indians had 'bred like rabbits.' He opposed Indian independence and called Gandhi a 'half-naked fakir.' Ask: how does the full record of a figure change how we read their most celebrated speech? Can someone be genuinely heroic in one context and responsible for atrocities in another? What do we leave out when we teach Churchill's speeches without his record in India?
systems_addressed: nationalism; imperialism; white supremacy; colonialism

title: Sandra Harding — 'Is Science Multicultural?' (on situated knowledge)
author: Sandra Harding
excerpt: Modern sciences have been imperial sciences, dependent on the vast labor of non-European peoples and the resources of their lands, developed within and in support of imperial projects, and systematically dismissing, excluding, and appropriating the knowledge traditions of non-European peoples.
topic: Science, knowledge production, colonialism, Indigenous knowledge, feminist epistemology
standards: APW U9; NYS 12.G5; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Sandra Harding, 'Is Science Multicultural? Challenges, Resources, Opportunities, Uncertainties,' Configurations, vol. 2, no. 2 (1994). Johns Hopkins University Press.
equity_note: Harding argues that science isn't 'view from nowhere' — it is always produced from somewhere, by someone, in a particular social context. European science developed in the context of colonialism, used colonial resources and labor, and systematically dismissed Indigenous knowledge systems that in many cases proved more effective (quinine, vaccines derived from Indigenous knowledge, agricultural techniques, etc.). Ask: if scientific knowledge is always situated, does that mean all knowledge is equally valid? What's the difference between acknowledging that science has a social context and rejecting the value of scientific method entirely?
systems_addressed: imperialism; colonialism; white supremacy; capitalism; environmental racism

title: Rachel Carson — Silent Spring (opening chapter: 'A Fable for Tomorrow')
author: Rachel Carson
excerpt: There was once a town in the heart of America where all life seemed to live in harmony with its surroundings… Then a strange blight crept over the area and everything began to change. Some evil spell had silenced the voices of spring in the birds. The farmers spoke of much illness among their families.
topic: Environmental movement, pesticides, corporate power, science as resistance, ecological crisis
attribution: Rachel Carson, Silent Spring (1962), Ch. 1: 'A Fable for Tomorrow.' Houghton Mifflin.
equity_note: Carson's book launched the modern environmental movement and led directly to the ban on DDT and the creation of the EPA. The chemical industry called her hysterical, a communist, and questioned whether an unmarried woman should be making public policy pronouncements. She was dying of cancer while writing it and knew it. She connected corporate profit motives to environmental destruction with scientific rigor and literary power. Ask: what made her arguments threatening enough to produce this level of personal attack? What does the nature of the attack — focused on her gender and marital status — tell us about how power responds to dissent?
systems_addressed: environmental racism; capitalism; class exploitation; corporate power

title: Blanche Bruce — Senate Speech on the Exclusion of Black Americans from the Electoral Process
author: Blanche Kelso Bruce
excerpt: I have confidence, not only in my country and her institutions, but in the endurance, capacity, and destiny of my people. We will, as opportunity offers and ability serves, seek our places, sometimes in the field of letters, arts, science, and the profofessions. More frequently mechanical pursuits will attract and elicit our efforts; more still of my people will find employment and livelihood as the cultivators of the soil.
topic: Reconstruction, Black voting rights, white supremacy, democracy, electoral fraud
attribution: Blanche Kelso Bruce, speech to the United States Senate, Washington D.C., March 31, 1876. Congressional Record, 44th Congress, 1st Session, pp. 2101-2106.
equity_note: Blanche Bruce was the first Black American to serve a full term in the U.S. Senate — elected from Mississippi in 1874. He was born enslaved. He served during Reconstruction and watched the federal government systematically abandon Black Southerners to white supremacist violence. His speech protesting electoral fraud and violence against Black voters in Mississippi is one of the most important documents of Reconstruction. Ask: what does it mean that a man born enslaved served in the U.S. Senate less than 15 years later — and that it would be another century before another Black senator from the Deep South was elected?
systems_addressed: anti-Blackness; white supremacy; democracy; settler colonialism

title: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie — 'The Danger of a Single Story' (TED Talk)
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
excerpt: The single story creates stereotypes, and the problem with stereotypes is not that they are untrue, but that they are incomplete. They make one story become the only story… The consequence of the single story is this: it robs people of dignity. It makes our recognition of our equal humanity difficult.
topic: Narrative, power, Africa, colonialism, representation, storytelling, empathy
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; Global II; APUSH P9
attribution: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, 'The Danger of a Single Story,' TED Global, Oxford, July 2009. TED Talks.
equity_note: Adichie's TED Talk has been viewed over 30 million times and is one of the most assigned texts in American schools. It argues that when one story is told about a person, place, or people — especially a story told by those with power — it flattens the full human complexity of its subjects. She uses her own experience as a Nigerian woman encountering Western single stories about Africa, and her American roommate's single story about Nigeria. Ask: what is the 'single story' told in your history textbook about Africa? About the Middle East? About Indigenous peoples? What would it take to tell multiple stories?
systems_addressed: white supremacy; anti-Blackness; imperialism; colonialism; nationalism

title: Vandana Shiva — 'Monocultures of the Mind' (on biodiversity and knowledge)
author: Vandana Shiva
excerpt: The monoculture of the mind makes the dominant system seem like the only possible world, and all alternatives disappear from the mind simultaneously with their disappearance from the world.
topic: Biodiversity, Indigenous knowledge, monoculture, capitalism, colonialism, food sovereignty
standards: APW U9; NYS 10.7; Global II Enduring Issues
attribution: Vandana Shiva, Monocultures of the Mind: Perspectives on Biodiversity and Biotechnology (1993), Ch. 1. Zed Books.
equity_note: Shiva argues that the 'Green Revolution' — celebrated as solving world hunger — actually destroyed agricultural biodiversity, displaced subsistence farmers, increased dependence on corporate chemicals and seeds, and concentrated food production in the hands of multinational corporations. She connects monocultures of plants to monocultures of thought: the replacement of diverse Indigenous knowledge systems with a single Western scientific framework. Ask: what does it mean when 'solving' a problem (hunger) produces new forms of the same problem (dependence, displacement)? Who benefits and who loses from the Green Revolution?
systems_addressed: capitalism; colonialism; environmental racism; neocolonialism; imperialism

title: Wole Soyinka — Nobel Prize Lecture (on African literature and tyranny)
author: Wole Soyinka
excerpt: I stand here today as the latest beneficiary of a vision that began not on this podium but in the living habits of a continent — an ancient, creative, productive continent whose civilizations antedate the rest of the world's by millennia, but a continent at present wracked by the most VIRULENT of distortions of the human potential.
topic: African literature, colonialism, tyranny, Yoruba mythology, Nigeria, political resistance
attribution: Wole Soyinka, Nobel Prize in Literature lecture, Stockholm, December 8, 1986. Nobel Foundation archives at nobelprize.org.
equity_note: Soyinka was the first African to win the Nobel Prize for Literature — in 1986. He spent two years in solitary confinement under the Nigerian military dictatorship. His Nobel lecture is a direct challenge to the European literary tradition's claim to universality, centering African civilization and Yoruba mythology as equal sources of human meaning. He used his Nobel platform to denounce apartheid South Africa — the Nobel committee was uncomfortable. Ask: when an African writer stands at the Nobel podium and says African civilizations predate Europe's — what is he claiming, and why does it matter to say it in Stockholm?
systems_addressed: colonialism; anti-Blackness; white supremacy; imperialism; authoritarianism

title: Tsitsi Dangarembga — Nervous Conditions (excerpt: on the colonized mind)
author: Tsitsi Dangarembga
excerpt: I was not sorry when my brother died. Nor am I apologising for my callousness, as you may define it, my lack of feeling. For me, his death was a welcome event. My mother was not so sanguine. She wanted to go to the funeral.
topic: Colonialism, Zimbabwe, women, education, identity, cultural displacement, resistance
standards: APW U8; APW U9; NYS 10.6; Global II
attribution: Tsitsi Dangarembga, Nervous Conditions (1988), opening. Women's Press, London.
equity_note: Nervous Conditions was the first novel published in English by a Black Zimbabwean woman — in 1988. Its title comes from Fanon's preface to The Wretched of the Earth: 'The condition of native is a nervous condition.' The narrator's brother's death opens up her own opportunity for education — which she pursues while watching it simultaneously destroy her cousin's sense of self. Ask: when education requires adopting the values, language, and worldview of the colonizer, what is the cost of getting educated? Dangarembga herself was arrested in 2020 at a pro-democracy protest in Zimbabwe at age 60. The nervous conditions are not historical.
systems_addressed: colonialism; heteropatriarchy; white supremacy; anti-Blackness; class exploitation

title: John Ross — Letter to Congress Protesting Indian Removal
author: John Ross (Principal Chief, Cherokee Nation)
excerpt: We are stripped of every attribute of freedom and eligibility for legal self-defence. Our property may be plundered before our eyes; violence may be committed on our persons; even our lives may be taken away, and there is none to regard our complaints. We are denationalized; we are disenfranchised.
topic: Indian Removal, Cherokee Nation, settler colonialism, treaty rights, democracy
standards: APUSH P4; NYS 11.2; APUSH U4; Grade 8 SS
attribution: John Ross, letter to the United States Senate and House of Representatives, September 28, 1836. Reprinted in Gary Moulton, The Papers of Chief John Ross, Vol. 1 (1985). University of Oklahoma Press.
equity_note: Ross wrote this after the fraudulent Treaty of New Echota (1835) was signed by a small faction without tribal authorization. He gathered 15,000 Cherokee signatures on a petition to Congress — they were ignored. Ross survived the Trail of Tears and continued to lead the Cherokee Nation for decades. Pairs directly with your Indian Removal Act (p022) and Major Ridge's treaty support speech (p023) — giving students all three positions: the US government, the minority of Cherokees who signed the treaty, and the vast majority who refused.
